title: Algorithmically Assisting Early Child Development; Propagation of Gambling Through Digital Devices
abstract: Digital technologies such as the internet, computers, and smartphones are able to connect the world such that people can talk to each other no matter where they are in the globe or simply look up any question they might have and have it answered. Yet at the same time various indicators of health, both physical and psychological, have deteriorated year after year in every age group and every part of the world according to agencies such as the WHO. This decline in health is also accompanied by a rise in various problems for people such as depression, suicide, chronic health conditions, and general unhappiness and dissatisfaction. My problem frame which both my technical paper and my STS research paper aim to address is the decline of mental in physical health, by examining different aspects digital technologies that are contributing to said decline. My STS research paper looks at how gambling has become more easily accessible through computers and mobile devices, which has made it easier for people to become addicted to it, negatively affecting their mental and financial health. My technical report details an application I helped develop that would help children and adolescents engage in more physical activity, with the aim of reducing the chance of them developing negative health conditions. My technical report addresses the work I did over the summer of 2024, working as a software development intern in order to build an application for early child development. In my report, I show my findings on how multiple sources, such as the UN, agree that there is a global drop the amount of physical activity done by children and adolescents, which is negatively correlated with cell phone use; furthermore, this has also led to an increase in the presence of chronic health conditions, earlier deaths, as well as worse mental health overall. The application being developed is meant to somewhat remedy this problem by allowing teachers and parents to easily give their children a short list of activities, ranging from painting or walking to pushups, squats, or running; furthermore, during development we were in constant talk with teachers and health professionals who provided feedback on ways the application could be improved. My STS thesis examines a few cases where gambling has become more widespread via various computer and mobile applications. Specifically, my paper discusses the rise of gambling in videogames, sports, as well as elections. Videogames that contain gambling generate much larger revenues than those who do not, and therefore publishers are incentivized to include these sorts of mechanics in their games. Sports gambling is an enormous industry that was only legalized in 2018, yet as of 2025 the average monthly wages combined across all platforms are in the billions. Election gambling was legalized in 2024 and could potentially pose another threat to the democratic process. Year over year, the number of people gambling as a whole, as well as the number of problem gamblers have continued to rise. With this, there has similarly been a decrease in people’s financial and mental health. According to my research, people that engage in gambling are more likely to suffer from depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts, as well as other negative health effects. Similarly, they are also more likely to default on their debt, and miss payments, or take out debt consolidation loans. Since the legalization of sports gambling, the number of calls to gambling call centers has nearly doubled every year since, and an increasing number of callers are minors or young adults. Both the technical solution and STS research paper have been unable to majorly contribute to a solution for the problem of decreasing mental and physical health. The technical solution is still under development and is yet to be deployed or tested. The STS research problem is similarly too complex to be easily solved, but various solutions that have worked in the past, such as banning gambling advertisements, stricter age verification, and limiting access to gambling applications on mobile devices would all see a decrease in the amount of gambling. In either case, the topic of how computers and mobile devices can impact a society’s health should be further studied. I would like to thank my STS professor, Caitlin Wylie, as well as my fellow classmates for helping me build and proofread my thesis. I would also like to thank George Prusiyski for guiding me through my internship and helping me learn the technical skills needed to develop the aforementioned application.

title: A behavioural trial of voluntary opt-out pre-commitment for online wagering in Australia
abstract: The study consisted of three key elements including a literature review of key insight on behavioural change, in particular as applied to gambling, a discrete choice experiment, and a randomised controlled trial. The research found that only a minority of regular gamblers had deposit limits in place though most gamblers that had limits found them useful. Higher-risk gamblers are more likely to set limits, though many do not want to limit their gambling. Gamblers may not set limits as they are easier to circumvent and not all gamblers are aware they can set limits. The limit type was the most influential message feature, followed (in order) by terminology and purpose, information to help set limits, message personalisation, message framing and message targeting. Receiving the optimal message had no significantly better effect on participants’ attitudes towards, intention to set, or actually setting of a deposit limit. Initiating a deposit or other type of limit during the four-week RCT period had a small but significant effect on decreasing the frequency of race betting, but no significant effect on sports betting frequency, betting expenditure or the experience of gambling harms.

title: Boltzmann-Informed Probabilities
abstract: Traditional interpretations of probability, whether frequentist or subjective, make no reference to the concept of energy. In this paper, we propose that assigning hypothetical energy levels to the outcomes of a random variable can yield improved probability estimates. We apply this Boltzmann-informed approach to the context of sports betting and analyze five seasons of the English Premier League data. It was found that when used to compute the Kelly criterion, Boltzmann-informed probabilities consistently outperform probabilities derived from the original betting odds. These findings demonstrate the value of integrating energy-informed probabilities into studying complex social systems.

title: Financial inducements in gambling marketing: An information disclosure proposal to inform gamblers of their true economic value
abstract: Financial inducements such as free bets are frequently-used gambling marketing offerswhich temporarily improve a gambler’s usual pattern of risk and potential return. Previous research has shown that there are up to 15 distinct types of financial inducements incommon use, and that gamblers frequently misunderstand inducements’ play-through requirements and other complex terms and conditions. The Australian government has therefore recently banned play-through requirements for inducements shown to new customers,and the Great British regulator the Gambling Commission has recently announced a maximum play-through requirement of 10 times. The present work describes an alternativeand yet potentially complementary approach based on disclosing financial inducements’true economic value to gamblers. This approach can be motivated by the fact that financialinducements are not intrinsically harmful, and an understanding of their value has beenexploited for profit by some gamblers via techniques called “bonus hunting” and “matchedbetting”. Disclosure-based approaches can be designed to reflect the average losses implied by any play-through requirements, as well as any other terms and conditions whichaffect their economic value. Disclosure-based approaches for protecting consumers fromthe potential harms of financial inducements should be subject to further research and policy consideration.

title: Not always as advertised: Different effects from viewing safer gambling (harm prevention) adverts on gambling urges.
abstract: Public concern around gambling advertising in the UK has been met not by government action but by industry self-regulations, such as a forthcoming voluntary ban on front-of-shirt gambling sponsorship in Premier League soccer. "Safer gambling" (harm prevention) adverts are one recent example, and are TV commercials which inform viewers about gambling-related harm. The present work is the first independent evaluation of safer gambling adverts by both gambling operators and a charity called GambleAware. In an online experiment, we observed the change in participants' (N = 2,741) Gambling Urge Scale (GUS) scores after viewing either: a conventional financial inducement gambling advert, a gambling operator's safer gambling advert, an advert from the GambleAware "bet regret" campaign, an advert from the GambleAware "stigma reduction" campaign, or a control advert that was not about gambling. Relative to a neutral control advert, GUS scores increased after viewing a financial inducement or an operator's safer gambling advert. In comparison to the neutral control condition, GUS score changes were similar after viewing a bet regret advert, but showed a significant decrease after viewing a stigma reduction advert. Those at higher risk of harm reported larger decreases in GUS after watching a bet regret or stigma reduction advert. Overall, this study introduced a novel experimental paradigm for evaluating safer gambling adverts, uncovered a potential downside from gambling operators' safer gambling adverts, and revealed variation in the potential effectiveness of charity-delivered safer gambling adverts.

title: Greater impulsivity is associated with a reduced propensity to cash out of bets
abstract: A common feature of contemporary sports-betting apps is ‘instant cash-out’, which allows users to settle a bet early in exchange for a discounted immediate payout. Despite high prevalence and links with gambling-related harm, relatively little is known about how personality traits associated with gambling, such as impulsivity, predict instant cash-out usage. To address this question, we recruited 145 general-population adult participants (69 men, 66 women, 10 non-binary or undisclosed; Mage = 36.3, SD = 10.7; participants resided in Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, the UK, or the USA) to complete five self-report questionnaires related to impulsivity, as well as the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI), and a validated cognitive task measuring individual differences in cash-out frequency. We then assessed how cash-out frequency in the behavioral task was associated with both self-reported impulsivity and PGSI. We found that cash-out frequency was negatively correlated both with PGSI scores and with a number of impulsivity-related traits including Dysfunctional Impulsivity, Lack of Premeditation, Positive Urgency, Sensation Seeking, and Fun Seeking. An exploratory factor analysis revealed that higher scores on a latent ‘Dysfunctional Impulsivity’ factor were negatively associated with cash-out frequency overall, whereas higher scores on an ‘Inhibition and Inflexibility’ factor predicted higher cash-out frequency specifically for bets with a low win probability. Taken together, results suggest that instant cash-out may primarily appeal to less impulsive people and those with lower PGSI scores. This raises the possibility that instant cash-out may specifically facilitate increased gambling behaviors among people with less prior experience of gambling.

title: Australia’s major sports codes are considered not-for-profits – is it time for them to pay up?
abstract: This article examines whether professional sport in Australia should receive a tax exemption as a not-for-profit organisation. The article examines the large revenues of the Australian Football League and the National Rugby League and their clubs and the reliance on sports gambling revenue. The research proposes the introduction of an unrelated income business income tax for the commercial income not related to the promotion of sport.

title: Gokken op e-sports, een gewoon spelletje? Een onderzoek naar toegang, drijfveren en consumptiepatronen
abstract: Over the past years, the options to place a wager on a bookmaker platform have broadened substantially, from being merely focused on traditional forms of sports to almost any type of competitive event related or unrelated to sports (Hing, Thorne, Russell, et al., 2024). While many of these new 'bettable' events remain marginally present and seem only requested by some heavy bettors (Newall, Walasek, Kiesel, et al., 2021), one notable exception are competitive video gaming tournaments, also known as cyber sports (Tang, Kim-wau Sum, Li, et al., 2023) or esports, short for electronic sports (Rogers, 2019). A unique, distinguishing feature of the esports betting phenomenon is that it is a form of third-order gameplay (cf. Kido Lopez, 2023); it is a game (i.e., betting) based on a game (i.e., competition) of games (i.e. video games). Put differently, inherent to esports betting is that it brings together three type of games - video games, sports and gambling (image 2). In line with Lopez-Gonzalez & Griffiths (2016:3), one could see this as a clear example of convergence: "a horizontal integration and collision of adjacent industry sectors". In this case, it is about the [RDC1] convergence[BZ2] of the video games, sports and gambling industries into something new. Surprisingly, however, the empirical and theoretical knowledge gained so far has been rather limited, This is in sharp contrast with research into other gaming-gambling convergence dynamics, such as the emergence of loot boxes or simulated gambling games (Mattinen, Macey & Hamari, 2023). In addition, when considering the scarcely available insights at hand, it becomes clear that the focus of most esports betting research is skewed towards particular (recurring) research questions, approaches, samples and settings (Lawn et al., 2020). It is particularly striking to see that, exceptions put aside (e.g., Yüce, Gökce Yüce, Katirci, et al., 2023), most studies are very traditionally designed around surveys, individualize the phenomenon as a merely psychological construct, and, while doing so, are often focused on Anglo-Saxon consumers and research settings. While these insights are all valuable in their own right and have provided a first insight in, among others, the demographic profile of the esports bettor (e.g., Gainsbury et al., 2017a-b), its motivations or the associated harms (e.g., Greer, Hing, Browne, et al., 2023), betting strategies (e.g., Sweeney, Tuttle, & Berg, 2021), or media use of these consumers (e.g., Macey & Hamari, 2018a-b), they also come with some issues. First, by merely having focused on Anglo-Saxon esports betting consumers, we currently only get a very limited picture of what esports betting entails in other nations or cultures. Despite their potential theoretical relevance, one cannot assume that many of the insights from a USA- and/or UK-context can just be translated into policies of other national jurisdictions, which have other gambling histories (Breuil, 2018), gambling rules (Hoekx, 2011) and/or values at stake (e.g., Hofstede, 2011). Second, the current state of the art has left many questions unanswered beyond the level of the individual. As research has shown, gambling, like other risky product consumption, is more than just an individual matter and also needs a thorough investigation from other levels of investigation, in particular from the level of the environment and product / technology (cf. Zinberg, 1984; Geeraerts, Wijgaerts, Claessens, et al., 2018). Third, and related to the former, two not many of the obtained insights seem to have been thoroughly replicated or triangulated with the methodological apparatus at our disposal, making us question whether some of the conclusions currently made about esports betting are reliable and valid (Wohl, Tabri, & Zelenski, 2019). The purpose of this doctoral dissertation, therefore, is to offer a complementary take towards the study of esports betting by: • Location-wise, changing 'where' and 'who' to focus on, shifting our attention to a geographically understudied, non-Anglo-Saxon research setting - Belgium (Lawn et al., 2020); • Topic-wise, expanding 'what' to investigate, by widening the scope towards both the environment, the product and the individual consumer, paying attention to structural and agentic properties of the Belgian gambling landscape (Giddens, 1984). • Method-wise, proposing new avenues on 'how' to do research, producing both novel and replicated insights into the Belgian esports betting landscape (Wohl, Tabri and Zelenski (2019). This endeavor will be reported and showcased throughout four empirical standalone chapters, all based on published (peer-reviewed) or ongoing research conducted between 2019 and 2025 (i.e., 'when').

title: APOSTAS ESPORTIVAS E INTERFERÊNCIA DE RESULTADOS
abstract: O aumento das apostas esportivas trouxe grandes ganhos econômicos para diversas empresas, mas também fez surgir problemas éticos e operacionais para o futebol profissional. Este artigo disserta sobre a ação intencional de jogadores em situações e eventos isolados, como faltas intencionais ou recebimento de cartões propositais, prática que busca beneficiar pessoas que estão supostamente ligadas as apostas. Embora não altere o resultado do jogo, essa prática criminosa prejudica não só a confiança no esporte, mas também a fé do público que começa a duvidar da veracidade das ações no campo. O objetivo deste estudo é verificar os efeitos éticos, sociais e financeiros dessa atividade e sugerir maneiras de reduzir problemas. Os métodos usados incluíram uma leitura de livros sobre espírito esportivo, regras de jogos a dinheiro e casos documentados de interferência. Também olhamos dados sobre o mercado de apostas esportivas e o aumento de modelos que deixam apostar em eventos específicos durante uma competição. Os achados indicam que essa prática, mesmo não sendo tão clara como a troca dos resultados, machuca muito a imagem dos jogadores e clubes e diminui o ͏interesse pelo futebol para fãs e patrocinadores. Além disso os mercados com pouca regulação são mais abertos a tais ações aumentando os danos econômicos e éticos. Conclui-se que a adoção de tecnologias avançadas para monitorar comportamentos suspeitos, a regulamentação mais rígida do mercado de apostas e a promoção de educação ética para atletas são essenciais para reduzir os efeitos dessas ações. Tais medidas visam proteger a integridade esportiva, assegurando a confiança do público e a sustentabilidade econômica do futebol.

title: At the limit of reason: identification and love for the club as triggers for sports betting addiction
abstract: This study investigated whether fans with stronger identification and love for their club engage more in sports betting, considering emotional bonds as potential triggers for risky behaviors. The research was conducted with football fans from Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, using a quantitative approach, descriptive design, and primary data collected through an online survey. The sample consisted of 400 respondents recruited through non-probabilistic snowball sampling. Validated psychometric scales were used to measure club identification, brand love, and betting involvement, in a five-point Likert format. The reliability of the instruments was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, which yielded satisfactory values. Analyses included descriptive statistics, internal consistency assessment of the scales, and simple linear regression estimated by Ordinary Least Squares (OLS). The results indicated that club identification directly influences brand love and has positive effects on betting frequency and addiction. Brand love was also a significant predictor of these behaviors, suggesting that intense affective bonds may trigger risky practices. Betting addiction was found to be a determinant of betting frequency among fans. These findings highlight the importance of emotional dimensions in understanding sports consumer behavior, particularly in activities with psychological and financial impacts. From a practical perspective, the results contribute to ethical reflections on the role of clubs, agencies, and platforms in fostering harmful behaviors, reinforcing the need for regulations that prioritize mental health and protect vulnerable audiences. Finally, limitations related to the sampling method and the exclusive use of self-report scales are acknowledged, and future research is recommended to include qualitative methods and expand the sample to other regions and social profiles.

title: Regulatory philosophies in the digital age: comparing the Malta Gaming Authority and UK Gambling Commission
abstract: This comparative analysis examines the contrasting regulatory philosophies of the Malta Gaming Authority (MGA) and UK Gambling Commission (UKGC), two leading European gambling regulators representing fundamentally different approaches to digital gambling oversight. Through systematic comparison of their legislative frameworks, licensing regimes, player protection measures, and enforcement mechanisms, this study reveals how jurisdictional priorities shape regulatory architecture. The UKGC has evolved towards prescriptive consumer protection measures for the UK domestic market, implementing comprehensive responsible gambling requirements including affordability checks and centralised self-exclusion systems. Conversely, the MGA has positioned itself as an international licensing hub, prioritising regulatory flexibility through a technology-neutral framework designed to attract global operators while maintaining baseline protection standards. The research demonstrates that the UKGC's domestic focus enables intensive harm prevention but potentially limits innovation, while the MGA's international approach fosters economic development but constrains consumer protection innovation due to regulatory competition pressures. These findings illuminate the central tension in modern gambling regulation between comprehensive consumer protection and market facilitation, with each authority representing distinct resolutions reflecting their unique institutional contexts and economic priorities.Keywords: gambling regulation, Malta Gaming Authority, UK Gambling Commission, regulatory philosophy, consumer protection, responsible gambling, player protection, licensing regimes, enforcement mechanisms, regulatory frameworks, international licensing, digital gambling, regulatory comparisonIntroductionThe regulation of gambling in the digital age presents unique challenges that demand sophisticated regulatory responses (Kingma, 2020). This comparative analysis examines two leading European regulators, the Malta Gaming Authority (MGA) and the UK Gambling Commission (UKGC), whose divergent approaches reflect fundamentally different regulatory philosophies. While the UKGC has evolved towards increasingly prescriptive consumer protection measures for its domestic market (National Audit Office, 2020), the MGA has positioned itself as an international licensing hub prioritising regulatory flexibility and market facilitation (Malta Gaming Authority, 2024). This comparison reveals how jurisdictional priorities shape regulatory architecture, with the UKGC's recent reforms emphasising responsible gambling and affordability checks whilst the MGA maintains a technology-neutral framework designed to attract international operators (House of Lords, 2020). Understanding these contrasting approaches provides critical insights into the broader evolution of gambling regulation from traditional oversight models to comprehensive digital-age frameworks that must balance consumer protection, market integrity, and economic objectives.Historical foundations and regulatory evolutionThe establishment and development of both regulatory authorities reflects their nations' distinct approaches to gambling oversight. The UK Gambling Commission emerged from the Gambling Act 2005, which received Royal Assent on 7 April 2005, replacing the Gaming Board for Great Britain that had regulated gambling since 1968 (UK Parliament, 2005). The UKGC assumed full regulatory powers on 1 September 2007, marking a fundamental shift towards a more comprehensive regulatory framework designed to address the challenges of modern gambling, particularly online operations (Gambling Commission, 2021). This transition represented a deliberate move from the restrictive approach of the Gaming Act 1968 towards a regulated market model that acknowledged gambling as a legitimate leisure activity requiring robust consumer protection (Miers, 2004).In contrast, Malta's regulatory journey began earlier and with a distinctly international focus. The Maltese authorities established the Lotteries and Gaming Authority (LGA) in 2001 under the Lotteries and Other Games Act, but the crucial development came in 2004 when Malta became the first EU Member State to specifically regulate remote gaming through the Remote Gaming Regulations (Cuschieri, 2019). This pioneering approach positioned Malta as a regulatory innovator, attracting international operators seeking EU market access. The authority underwent corporate rebranding in 2015, transforming from the LGA to the MGA to better represent its evolving role (Malta Gaming Authority, 2015). The most significant legislative development occurred with the Gaming Act 2018 (Chapter 583 of the Laws of Malta), which consolidated all previous gaming legislation under one comprehensive horizontal framework, coming into force on 1 August 2018 (Government of Malta, 2018).These historical trajectories reveal fundamental differences in regulatory philosophy. The UKGC's establishment followed extensive parliamentary debate about social responsibility and consumer protection, reflecting British public policy concerns about gambling-related harm (Orford et al., 2003). The Gambling Act 2005 established three licensing objectives that continue to guide UKGC operations: preventing gambling from being a source of crime or disorder, ensuring gambling is conducted fairly and openly, and protecting children and vulnerable persons (UK Parliament, 2005). These objectives embedded consumer protection at the heart of British gambling regulation.The MGA's evolution, conversely, reflects Malta's strategic economic positioning as a regulatory hub for international operators. The 2004 Remote Gaming Regulations demonstrated remarkable foresight in recognising online gambling's potential, establishing Malta as a preferred jurisdiction for operators seeking stable regulation and EU market access (Briguglio & Pace, 2004). The subsequent legislative consolidation in 2018 further enhanced this position by creating a technology-neutral regulatory framework that could adapt to emerging gaming technologies without requiring constant legislative revision (Ellul Schranz, 2024).Legislative architecture and regulatory frameworksThe legislative frameworks underpinning both authorities demonstrate their contrasting regulatory philosophies through structure and implementation mechanisms. The UKGC operates under a relatively straightforward legislative hierarchy centred on the Gambling Act 2005, supplemented by the License Conditions and Codes of Practice (LCCP) which possess binding force under Section 75 of the Act (Gambling Commission, 2024a). This framework received significant expansion through the Gambling (Licensing and Advertising) Act 2014, which extended UKGC jurisdiction to all operators targeting British consumers regardless of their location, effectively creating a comprehensive regulatory perimeter around the British market (Collins et al., 2015).The MGA employs a more complex three-tier regulatory structure that provides greater flexibility whilst maintaining comprehensive coverage. The primary tier comprises the Gaming Act 2018, establishing fundamental regulatory principles and the MGA's powers (Government of Malta, 2018). The secondary tier encompasses twelve subsidiary legislative instruments (S.L. 583.01 to 583.12) covering specific aspects from authorisation procedures to technical standards and tax regulations. The tertiary tier consists of MGA Directives and Guidelines that provide detailed operational requirements without requiring legislative amendment (Malta Gaming Authority, 2023a). This structure enables rapid regulatory adaptation to technological and market developments whilst maintaining legislative stability.The UKGC's approach emphasises prescriptive requirements with detailed specifications for operator conduct. The LCCP underwent substantial revision in October 2020, introducing 22 specific changes covering anti-money laundering procedures, customer interaction requirements, and data reporting obligations (Gambling Commission, 2020). The 2023 White Paper "High stakes: gambling reform for the digital age" proposes over 60 additional policy measures, demonstrating the UKGC's increasingly interventionist approach to market regulation (HM Government, 2023). These reforms reflect parliamentary and public pressure for stronger consumer protection measures, particularly regarding vulnerable gamblers and affordability assessments.The MGA's legislative framework prioritises regulatory efficiency and international compatibility. The consolidation under the Gaming Act 2018 eliminated fragmentation between different gaming verticals, creating uniform standards applicable across all gambling activities (Mondaq, 2023). This horizontal approach reduces regulatory complexity for operators whilst maintaining comprehensive oversight. The framework's technology neutrality ensures regulatory longevity, avoiding the need for constant legislative updates as new gaming technologies emerge (SOFTSWISS, 2025). This approach particularly benefits operators offering multiple gaming products or utilising innovative technologies like distributed ledger systems or cryptocurrencies.Licensing regimes and authorisation structuresThe licensing systems operated by both authorities reflect their distinct regulatory priorities and market orientations. The UKGC issues operating licenses across three main categories: remote licenses for online operations, non-remote licenses for physical premises, and ancillary licenses for supporting activities (Gambling Commission, 2024b). Within these categories exist numerous subcategoriesremote betting on real events, virtual events, betting intermediary services, remote casino, bingo, and lottery operations each require specific authorisation. The UKGC additionally mandates personal licenses for key management positions, with Personal Management Licenses required for chief executives, managing directors, board chairs, and compliance officers (Sumsub, 2024). This comprehensive approach ensures individual accountability alongside corporate responsibility.The MGA simplified its licensing structure through the 2018 reforms, establishing two primary license categories that reflect modern gaming industry structures.Business-to-Consumer (B2C) Gaming Service Licenses cover four types of gaming activities (Malta Gaming Authority, 2024a): Type 1 encompasses games of chance including casino games and virtual sports; Type 2 covers fixed-odds betting and sportsbooks; Type 3 includes peer-to-peer games, poker, and pool betting; Type 4 addresses controlled skill games including fantasy sports Business-to-Business (B2B) Critical Gaming Supply Licenses authorise the provision of essential gaming infrastructure, software, and platform services. This streamlined approach reduces administrative complexity whilst maintaining comprehensive regulatory coverage.Financial requirements for licensing demonstrate significant philosophical differences. The UKGC emphasises detailed financial assessments including three-year business projections, comprehensive source of funds verification, and ongoing financial monitoring through quarterly regulatory returns introduced in July 2024 (Next.io, 2024). These requirements reflect concerns about operator financial stability and the protection of customer funds. The MGA requires share capital ranging from €40,000 to €240,000 depending on license type, with annual fees between €3,000 and €35,000 plus monthly compliance contributions based on gaming revenue (ICLG, 2025). These lower financial barriers reflect Malta's strategy to attract smaller innovative operators whilst maintaining regulatory standards.The application processes further illustrate contrasting approaches. The UKGC's application procedure involves extensive documentation requirements including detailed policies and procedures demonstrating LCCP compliance, comprehensive anti-money laundering procedures, and technical standards compliance (Gambling Commission, 2024b). Processing times vary considerably depending on application complexity and the level of regulatory scrutiny required. The MGA operates through its electronic Licensee Portal with a standardised 12-16 week processing timeline, emphasising efficiency and predictability (Malta Gaming Authority, 2024b). The System Documentation Checklist provides clear technical requirements, enabling operators to prepare comprehensive applications that meet regulatory expectations.Player protection philosophies and implementationPlayer protection measures represent perhaps the starkest contrast between the two regulatory approaches, with the UKGC implementing increasingly prescriptive requirements whilst the MGA maintains a framework-based approach allowing operator flexibility. The UKGC's customer interaction requirements, strengthened through Social Responsibility Code 3.4.3, mandate specific interventions based on identified harm indicators (Gambling Commission, 2023). Operators must implement automated monitoring systems, conduct affordability assessments at Commission-set thresholds, and maintain detailed records of all customer interactions. The proposed implementation of "light touch" financial checks at £150 net deposits over 30 days and enhanced checks for customers losing £1,000 in 24 hours or £2,000 over 90 days represents unprecedented regulatory intervention in customer gambling behaviour.- (HM Government, 2023)The MGA's Player Protection Directive, whilst comprehensive, provides operators greater flexibility in implementation. Article 17A establishes minimum criteria including monitoring deposit and wagering frequency, multiple payment method usage, withdrawal reversals, and responsible gambling tool utilisation, but allows operators to develop tailored approaches within these parameters (Malta Gaming Authority, 2023b). The MGA introduced five specific markers of harm in 2023 amendments, providing clarity whilst maintaining operational flexibility. This approach recognises operator expertise in customer behaviour whilst ensuring minimum protection standards.Self-exclusion systems exemplify different regulatory strategies. The UKGC mandates participation in GAMSTOP, a centralised multi-operator self-exclusion scheme operational since March 2020, providing exclusion periods of six months, one year, or five years with automatic renewal options (iGaming Academy, 2024). All licensed operators must update exclusion lists every 24 hours, creating a comprehensive barrier for self-excluded individuals. The MGA currently operates through operator-specific self-exclusion systems as outlined in the Player Protection Directive, though market consultation indicates movement towards a unified system (Amber Gaming, 2023). The current approach allows exclusion by gaming vertical or website, with cross-brand exclusion applying when operators identify problem gambling indicators.Advertising restrictions further demonstrate regulatory divergence. title: Taxation as Gambling Harm Reduction or UK Treasury Imperative?
abstract: Working title: A Critical Analysis of the UK Government's 2025 Gambling Duty Reforms Through the Lens of Welfare Economics and Public Administration12 December 2025AbstractThis paper critically examines the United Kingdom Government's November 2025 reforms to gambling taxation, announced by Chancellor Rachel Reeves, which nearly doubled Remote Gaming Duty from 21% to 40% and increased online betting duty from 15% to 25%. Drawing on welfare economics theory, particularly Pigouvian taxation frameworks, and public administration scholarship, this analysis interrogates whether these reforms constitute a genuine public health intervention designed to reduce gambling-related harm or represent a fiscal strategy primarily motivated by Treasury revenue requirements. The paper examines the interplay between increased taxation, existing Know Your Customer (KYC) regulatory requirements, and the Online Safety Act 2023, arguing that the cumulative regulatory burden may produce unintended consequences, including accelerated migration to unlicensed black market operators. Through systematic analysis of government documentation, industry data, and academic literature, this study concludes that while the rhetorical framing emphasises harm reduction, the policy architecture reveals a fundamental tension between revenue optimisation and genuine public health objectives. The paper recommends a recalibration of policy priorities toward demand-side interventions and enhanced treatment infrastructure rather than supply-side taxation alone.Keywords: gambling taxation, Pigouvian tax, welfare economics, harm reduction, black market, regulatory policy, public health, UK gambling reform 1. IntroductionOn 26 November 2025, Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves delivered what has been described as the most significant restructuring of gambling taxation in the United Kingdom since the Gambling Act 2005. The reforms, announced as part of the Autumn Budget, increased Remote Gaming Duty (RGD) from 21% to 40% effective April 2026, with General Betting Duty for online betting rising from 15% to 25% from April 2027 (HM Treasury, 2025). The Chancellor justified these increases by asserting that 'remote gaming is associated with the highest levels of harm' and that the reforms would generate 'over £1 billion per year by 2031' (Reeves, 2025). This dual framing—emphasising both harm reduction and revenue generation—raises fundamental questions about the true objectives underlying these policy changes.The gambling industry in the United Kingdom represents a substantial economic sector, generating gross gambling yield (GGY) of £15.6 billion in the financial year ending March 2024 (Gambling Commission, 2024). Within this market, online gambling has experienced particularly rapid growth, with remote gaming yields increasing by 61% over the preceding five years (Department for Culture, Media and Sport, 2025). This growth has been accompanied by increasing public health concerns, with the Gambling Survey for Great Britain (GSGB) reporting that 2.7% of adults scored in the problem gambling range on the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI), equating to approximately 1.4 million individuals (Gambling Commission, 2024).This paper examines the 2025 gambling tax reforms through the theoretical frameworks of welfare economics and public administration, interrogating whether these measures represent a coherent public health strategy or a fiscally-motivated intervention dressed in the language of harm reduction. The analysis proceeds in several stages: first, examining the theoretical foundations of taxation as a tool for addressing harmful consumption; second, analysing the specific policy architecture of the 2025 reforms; third, evaluating the likely behavioural responses and market dynamics, including black market migration; and finally, assessing the alignment between stated objectives and probable outcomes.2. Theoretical Framework: Taxation and the Correction of Market Failures2.1 Pigouvian Taxation and Externality CorrectionThe theoretical justification for taxing harmful commodities derives primarily from the work of Arthur Cecil Pigou, whose seminal contribution established that taxation could serve as a mechanism for correcting market failures arising from negative externalities (Pigou, 1920). In the Pigouvian framework, the optimal tax rate is set equal to the marginal external cost imposed on third parties, thereby 'internalising' externalities and aligning private incentives with social welfare (Barnett, 1980). This approach has been applied extensively to tobacco, alcohol, and carbon emissions, with varying degrees of success (Lucas, 2024).Applied to gambling, the Pigouvian framework suggests that taxation should reflect the social costs generated by gambling-related harm. Public Health England estimated these costs at £1.27 billion annually in England alone, including £619.2 million attributable to gambling-related suicide (PHE, 2021). The Office for Health Improvement and Disparities subsequently revised this estimate to between £1.05 and £1.77 billion (OHID, 2023). If taxation were genuinely calibrated to internalise these externalities, the rate would be determined by the marginal social cost per unit of gambling activity—a calculation that does not appear in any Treasury documentation accompanying the 2025 reforms.The distinction between Pigouvian taxes and 'sin taxes' is relevant here. While Pigouvian taxes are theoretically calibrated to match external costs, sin taxes are often set at levels designed to maximise revenue while suppressing demand—a dual objective that creates inherent tensions (Tax Foundation, 2024). As Walker and Barnett (1999) observed in their critique of gambling cost-benefit analyses, 'simply because the government spends money on something does not necessarily imply that the expenditure represents a social cost'. This conceptual confusion pervades much policy discourse on gambling taxation.2.2 Behavioural Economics and the Limits of Price MechanismsContemporary behavioural economics has complicated the classical economic assumption that price increases straightforwardly reduce demand for harmful goods. Research on addiction suggests that individuals suffering from gambling disorder exhibit bounded rationality and time-inconsistent preferences, making them less responsive to price signals than recreational gamblers (Fiedler, 2021). This implies that taxation may disproportionately burden problem gamblers—those least able to moderate their behaviour—while having limited deterrent effects on the most harmful forms of consumption.Furthermore, the price elasticity of demand for gambling products varies significantly across market segments. Evidence from the UK presented by Paton et al. (2004) suggests that sports betting volumes are highly sensitive to tax changes, though the elasticity varies by product type and consumer demographic. Online casino products, particularly slots—which generate the highest harm according to NHS Digital (2023)—may exhibit different elasticity profiles than sports betting, yet the 2025 reforms apply near-uniform rate increases across these distinct product categories.2.3 Public Administration and Policy CoherenceFrom a public administration perspective, effective policy requires alignment between stated objectives, policy instruments, and implementation mechanisms (Hood, 1983). The 2025 gambling reforms exist within a complex regulatory ecosystem that includes the Gambling Act 2005, the 2023 White Paper 'High Stakes: Gambling Reform for the Digital Age', ongoing Gambling Commission enforcement activity, and the statutory gambling levy introduced in 2025. Coherent governance demands that these instruments work synergistically rather than at cross-purposes.The policy architecture reveals potential contradictions. If the primary objective is harm reduction, taxation represents an indirect and inefficient mechanism compared to direct interventions such as stake limits, mandatory breaks in play, or enhanced treatment provision. The government's simultaneous introduction of online slot stake limits (£5 for over-25s, £2 for 18-24 year-olds) from April 2025 suggests recognition of this principle, yet these measures operate independently of the taxation framework (Gambling Act 2005 (Operating Licence Conditions) (Amendment) Regulations 2024). 3. Critical Analysis of the 2025 Gambling Duty Reforms3.1 Revenue Projections and Fiscal MotivationThe Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) projected that the gambling duty reforms would raise £1.1 billion annually by 2029-30, with receipts increasing from £4 billion in 2025-26 to £6 billion by 2030-31 (OBR, 2025). Significantly, the OBR acknowledged that this figure would have reached £1.8 billion without anticipated 'behavioural changes'—a euphemism encompassing reduced betting volumes and migration to unlicensed operators. The government's own projections thus assume that substantial tax revenues will be lost to black market displacement, raising questions about whether revenue maximisation or harm reduction drives policy calibration.The timing and context of the reforms warrant scrutiny. The proposals were championed extensively by former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, who explicitly linked gambling taxation to funding for child poverty reduction through scrapping the two-child benefit cap (Brown, 2025). The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) estimated that reforms could generate £3.2 billion, sufficient to lift 500,000 children out of poverty (IPPR, 2025). This framing positions gambling taxation primarily as a revenue-raising mechanism for social expenditure rather than a targeted intervention against gambling harm.Brown argued that 'gambling won't build our country for the next generation, but children, freed from poverty, will' (Brown, 2025). While rhetorically compelling, this argument treats gambling taxation instrumentally—as a means to fund unrelated policy objectives—rather than as a calibrated response to the specific harms generated by gambling activity. The logical implication is troubling: successful harm reduction that substantially decreased gambling activity would simultaneously undermine funding for child poverty programmes, creating a perverse incentive structure.3.2 The Harm Reduction Rationale: Rhetoric and RealityChancellor Reeves's assertion that 'remote gaming is associated with the highest levels of harm' draws on substantial evidence. NHS Digital data indicates that problem gambling rates among online slots and casino players are eight times higher than in the general population (NHS Digital, 2023). The Treasury Select Committee, chaired by Dame Meg Hillier, endorsed the principle of risk-based taxation, concluding that 'the tax rate for remote betting, including highly addictive casino games, should reflect the harm it inflicts' (Treasury Select Committee, 2025).However, genuine harm reduction requires that taxation either reduces harmful consumption directly or generates hypothecated revenues for treatment and prevention. On the first criterion, evidence from European markets is mixed. Marionneau et al. (2024) conducted multivariate regression analysis across 29 European countries and found 'no evidence of a negative correlation between taxation rates and channelling rates'—suggesting higher taxes do not necessarily reduce gambling consumption. Their study concluded that 'channelling objectives are important for better regulation and harm reduction, but taxation levels do not appear to be correlated to the success of channelling policies'.On revenue hypothecation, the 2025 reforms introduced a separate statutory gambling levy (distinct from the duty increases) to fund research, prevention, and treatment. title: The Dark Side of KYC and Online Casino Regulation in the UK: A Systematic Review of Literature
abstract: IntroductionSince May 2019, the UK Gambling Commission's enhanced Know Your Customer requirements have created an unprecedented barrier between vulnerable populations and regulated gambling services, driving a 522% surge in black market gambling activity (IFHA, 2025) whilst 67% of self-excluded gamblers now circumvent protections entirely (Social Intent, 2024). Academic research reveals that these well-intentioned consumer protection measures have transformed into instruments of financial exclusion, disproportionately impacting unemployed individuals, disabled people, women without utility bills in their names, and cash-paid workers who cannot meet stringent documentation requirements.This systematic literature review examines how mandatory identity verification before any gambling activity - including demo games or marketing materials - has created a two-tier system where privileged populations access regulated services whilst marginalised communities are pushed towards dangerous unregulated alternatives. The evidence suggests that current KYC enforcement represents a fundamental misunderstanding of addiction psychology and harm reduction principles, prioritising regulatory compliance over the actual protection of working-class problem gamblers who face the greatest consequences from displacement to black market operators.Financial exclusion masquerading as consumer protectionThe UKGC's 2019 enhanced KYC requirements mandate comprehensive identity verification including government-issued identification, proof of address, and increasingly, affordability assessments through credit checks and banking data. Research from advocacy groups and academic institutions reveals these requirements systematically exclude vulnerable populations through documentation barriers that mirror broader patterns of financial exclusion.Women face particular challenges when utility bills and financial documents remain in their spouse's name, a pattern reflecting historical financial exclusion where only 77% of legal rights are enjoyed compared to men globally (World Bank, 2024). The World Bank's research on financial inclusion demonstrates how KYC requirements amplify existing gender inequalities, with married women often unable to provide the specific documentation formats required by automated verification systems (Mabrouk et al., 2023). This creates a cascade effect where those already marginalised by traditional financial systems face additional barriers to regulated gambling services.Disabled individuals encounter both digital and physical accessibility barriers throughout KYC processes. Despite the Equality Act 2010's requirements for reasonable adjustments, UKGC guidance contains "no stipulations regarding the rights of physically vulnerable individuals" within gambling contexts (Centre for American Progress, 2024). Academic research documents how digital-only verification processes exclude those with cognitive impairments, visual disabilities, or limited digital literacy, whilst the absence of assisted completion options or alternative formats violates fundamental accessibility principles. The cumulative effect is a system that discriminates against protected characteristics whilst claiming to offer universal protection.Cash-paid workers in construction, hospitality, and other sectors cannot provide the formal income verification increasingly required for affordability assessments. Research shows that financial exclusion disproportionately affects low-income households (Joseph Rowntree Foundation, 2023), with irregular payment patterns triggering enhanced due diligence requirements that assume criminality rather than recognising legitimate informal economy participation. Self-employed individuals face similar challenges, with fluctuating earnings and complex income documentation failing to fit standardised verification algorithms designed for regular salary earners.The displacement effect drives vulnerable gamblers undergroundAcademic literature on addiction psychology demonstrates that compulsive behaviours rarely cease when faced with barriers - instead, they find alternative expressions. Multiple studies confirm this displacement effect within UK gambling, with the most comprehensive data showing a 522% increase in unique customers visiting unlicensed betting sites between August 2021 and September 2024, compared to only 49% growth for licensed operators (IFHA, 2025).Fong's (2022) neurobiological research at UCLA reveals that gambling disorder involves dopamine pathways creating powerful compulsions where individuals "psychologically view gambling as the answer to their problems." When KYC barriers prevent access to regulated platforms, these compulsions don't disappear but redirect towards accessible alternatives. Cambridge University studies on "loss chasing" behaviour show that near-misses and perceived personal choice activate brain reward circuits (University of Cambridge, 2023), making gamblers more likely to circumvent barriers when blocked rather than reducing gambling activity.The displacement evidence is particularly stark among self-excluded individuals. The 2024 Social Intent report found that 67% of Gamstop self-exclusion users accessed black market websites to bypass restrictions, with over 420,000 UK schoolchildren potentially engaging in unregulated gambling. Academic reviews consistently show that individual-frame measures like KYC yield "small or even null results" compared to system-level interventions (ScienceDirect, 2019), with the World Health Organization (2023) noting that responsibility-shifting to consumers through such measures often fails whilst increasing stigma and reducing help-seeking behaviour.International evidence reinforces these findings. Netherlands data shows near parity between legal (€306m) and illegal (€305m) gambling spending in Q4 2024 after introducing monthly spending caps (Next.io, 2025), demonstrating immediate displacement effects from restrictive measures. The International Federation of Horseracing Authorities documented a major spike in unlicensed activity around April 2024, with 16.75% of visits to one major unlicensed operator coming directly from "not on Gamstop" referral sites specifically targeting excluded customers (IFHA, 2025).Search data reveals the migration to cryptocurrency gamblingGoogle Trends analysis and industry research reveal clear correlations between KYC enforcement milestones and increased searches for unregulated alternatives. The dichotomy between legitimate and black market gambling marketing is starkly illustrated by examining two contrasting approaches to online casino promotion.Sites focussed on the licensed "best casino sites" niche, such as BestCasinoSites.net, exclusively promote UKGC-licensed operators, emphasising regulatory compliance as a selling point (BestCasinoSites.net, 2025). The site prominently displays licensing information, stating "Our expert review team has thoroughly assessed each UK Gambling Commission (UKGC) licensed casino site" and highlights responsible gambling tools, customer protection measures, and regulatory oversight as key benefits for players.In stark contrast, platforms targeting users searching for keywords similar to "online casino no KYC" explicitly market the absence of these protections. Cointelegraph's "Best No KYC Casinos" guide directly appeals to KYC-excluded individuals with promotional language such as "skip the lengthy verification processes," "completely anonymous gaming," and "instant sign-up with an email and username" (Cointelegraph, 2025). The guide explicitly advertises crypto casinos that allow players to "enjoy safe and secure crypto casino games without the need for 'know your customer' procedures" and promises "no verification casinos allowing crypto."This contrast demonstrates how regulatory barriers have bifurcated online gambling marketing into distinct channels serving different populations - those who can access regulated services versus those systematically excluded by KYC requirements.Following the May 2019 mandatory verification implementation, searches for "casinos not on Gamstop" showed sustained growth, with content creators gaining "over one million views in a single month" promoting non-Gamstop casinos (iGaming Business, 2024). By 2024, 84% of gambling content creators surveyed were promoting black market sites (Deal Me Out, 2024). The divergence is particularly evident in affiliate marketing strategies: whilst sites like BestCasinoSites.net emphasise regulatory compliance, responsible gambling tools, and UKGC licensing as selling points, black market affiliates explicitly advertise the absence of these protections as benefits.The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated this trend, with BBC reporting online casino searches reaching "all-time high" during lockdown. Academic studies documented "sharp increases in internet searches for poker, slots, and bingo" during the first UK lockdown (PMC, 2023), whilst GambleAware noted a 193% increase in searches for online betting and virtual events within two weeks post-lockdown. This surge coincided with enhanced KYC enforcement as operators implemented stricter verification to manage increased volume.Cryptocurrency gambling represents the most significant displacement trend. Between 2019-2021, Bitcoin casino interest "quadrupled" according to industry analysis (Gambling Insider, 2024), with the number of crypto casinos serving UK customers increasing by 25% in one year through 2024 (South West Londoner, 2024). A 2024 YouGov poll found that 30% of UK online gamblers have tried cryptocurrency casinos, attracted by explicit "no ID checks, no verification" marketing (YouGov, 2024). The Cointelegraph guide exemplifies this marketing approach, promising "completely anonymous gaming" and "instant sign-up with an email and username" - features that directly appeal to individuals excluded by traditional KYC processes.Most concerning is how black market operators specifically target KYC-excluded individuals. Industry reports document 5 million clicks per month directed to black market sites via affiliate links (Deal Me Out, 2024), with 90% of content creators using unlicensed crypto platforms like BC.Game. YouTube creators openly acknowledge that "regulation has forced our hand; if we don't use crypto casinos we just can't compete," as viewers demand content featuring bonus buys and turbo spins banned under UK regulations (iGaming Business, 2024).Government recognition without meaningful reformThe UK government's position reveals awareness of displacement risks coupled with reluctance to address root causes. HMRC maintains that gambling winnings remain tax-free whether from licensed or unlicensed operators (GOV.UK, 2024), removing financial incentives for players to choose regulated options. Crucially, no criminal penalties exist for UK residents using unlicensed gambling sites for personal use (Online Betting UK, 2024), with enforcement focussed entirely on operators rather than players.Parliamentary debates reflect growing concern about KYC's discriminatory effects. A February 2024 Westminster Hall debate addressed a petition with over 200,000 signatures opposing financial risk checks as "inappropriate and discriminatory" (UK Parliament, 2024). MPs highlighted how affordability checks could discriminate against "self-employed, entrepreneurs and individuals with high wealth but low income," noting that credit data is "extremely unhelpful when it comes to people with irregular money flows" (Hansard, 2024).The 2023 Gambling Act Review White Paper explicitly acknowledges that "it would be undesirable for an illegal gambling market to grow," recognising unlicensed operators "do not comply with regulatory or tax obligations and seek to draw customers away from the legitimate sector" (GOV.UK, 2023). UKGC CEO Andrew Rhodes admits that unlicensed sites specifically target "people who are self-excluded or have otherwise had customer relationships terminated by operators" (SBC News, 2024).Yet despite this recognition, policy responses remain focussed on intensifying the very measures driving displacement. The August 2024 launch of financial risk check pilots at £500+ monthly losses, combined with online slot limits of £5 for over-25s and £2 for 18-24 year olds (UKGC, 2024), suggests continued adherence to restriction-based approaches despite evidence of their counterproductive effects. The Advertising Standards Authority struggles with limited jurisdiction over international influencers and encrypted messaging platforms, whilst £36.9 million in annual Remote Gaming Duty is lost to black market operators (Wiggin LLP, 2024).International evidence supports graduated risk-based approachesAcademic literature strongly endorses graduated KYC systems that balance harm reduction with accessibility. Meta-analyses of risk-based regulation demonstrate superior effectiveness compared to "one-size-fits-all" approaches, with European research indicating flexibility enhances compliance whilst reducing unnecessary burden on low-risk users.Financial services provide a proven model through tiered verification systems. Basic bank accounts allow simplified onboarding for low-risk customers with transaction limits around £50,000 annually, whilst enhanced verification applies only to higher-value accounts. Research shows these graduated systems improve financial inclusion (World Bank, 2024) whilst maintaining security standards, with only 0.3% of users exceeding reasonable deposit limits when studied across 47,000 accounts.International gambling jurisdictions demonstrate successful implementation of proportionate approaches. Sweden's Spelpaus system achieves 81% participation among treatment seekers through comprehensive coverage, whilst Finland's tiered verification based on transaction volume reduces barriers for casual players. The Netherlands licensing model employs risk-based verification with proportionate requirements, though recent monthly cap implementations show the dangers of overly restrictive measures.Studies on game-type differentiation reveal varying addiction risk profiles that could inform graduated approaches. Slots demonstrate the highest addiction potential due to speed and continuous play features, whilst strategic games like poker show some protective social elements. Norwegian research indicates time-based limits prove more effective than monetary restrictions alone (Harm Reduction Journal, 2023), with combined approaches (time plus monetary limits) showing greatest harm reduction potential. Yet current UK regulations apply uniform requirements regardless of game type or risk level.The social justice imperative for reformFrom a human rights perspective, current KYC implementation constitutes indirect discrimination violating principles of equal access to services. The Equality Act 2010 prohibits discrimination based on protected characteristics including disability, sex, and race - yet KYC requirements systematically exclude individuals with these characteristics through documentation barriers and inaccessible processes.The class dimension is particularly stark. Industry data shows "people who tend to lose the most money from online slots also tend to live in more deprived parts of the country" (UK Parliament, 2025), yet these same populations face the greatest barriers to regulated services. Working-class problem gamblers driven to black market alternatives encounter platforms with higher-risk game designs, no deposit limits, absent self-exclusion options, and zero dispute resolution mechanisms. When losses occur on unlicensed platforms, players have no legal recourse or consumer protections.Academic consensus supports harm reduction over prohibition, recognising that overly restrictive measures increase rather than decrease harm for vulnerable populations (Harvard Public Health, 2023). The evidence overwhelmingly indicates that well-intentioned consumer protections have transformed into instruments of exclusion, creating a two-tier system where privileged populations access safer regulated gambling whilst marginalised communities face dangerous unregulated alternatives.ConclusionThe systematic exclusion of vulnerable populations from regulated gambling services through enhanced KYC requirements represents a fundamental failure of consumer protection policy. Evidence from academic research, industry data, and government statistics demonstrates that current approaches drive problem gamblers towards black market alternatives rather than reducing harm. The 522% surge in unlicensed gambling activity (IFHA, 2025), coupled with 67% of self-excluded individuals circumventing protections (Social Intent, 2024), reveals displacement rather than prevention as the primary outcome of restrictive KYC enforcement.Reform requires acknowledging that addiction operates through neurobiological mechanisms impervious to administrative barriers (Fong, 2022). A genuinely protective regulatory framework would implement graduated, risk-based verification systems proven effective in financial services (World Bank, 2024), with basic access requiring minimal documentation whilst enhanced scrutiny applies only to high-risk behaviours. Universal deposit limits without full KYC, time-based controls, and comprehensive cross-operator monitoring could provide actual harm reduction whilst maintaining accessibility for vulnerable populations currently excluded from legal protections (Harm Reduction Journal, 2023). Without such reforms, KYC requirements will continue serving as instruments of discrimination, pushing those most in need of protection towards the very harms regulation claims to prevent.ReferencesBestCasinoSites.net (2025) Best Casino Sites – 2025 Ratings for UK Players.
